title: Laboratory Techniques II
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned 200-level Science Laboratory Technology curriculum building on SLT201: separation and purification techniques (chromatography, extraction, distillation, crystallization, sublimation), gravimetric analysis, basic colorimetry/spectrophotometry, electrophoresis, and sample preservation, all bench-technique oriented and distinct from SLT201's basic measurement/titration content.

questions.question: Chromatography separates the components of a mixture based on:
options: Differences in boiling point only
Differences in the relative affinity of components for a stationary phase versus a moving mobile phase
Differences in electrical conductivity
Differences in melting point only
questions.correct_answer: Differences in the relative affinity of components for a stationary phase versus a moving mobile phase
questions.explanation: All chromatographic methods separate mixture components by how strongly each is retained by the stationary phase compared with how readily it travels with the mobile phase.

questions.question: In thin-layer chromatography (TLC), the Rf value of a spot is calculated as:
options: Distance travelled by solvent front divided by distance travelled by the spot
Distance travelled by the spot divided by distance travelled by the solvent front
Distance travelled by the spot multiplied by the plate length
Time taken for the spot to travel divided by total run time
questions.correct_answer: Distance travelled by the spot divided by distance travelled by the solvent front
questions.explanation: Rf (retention factor) = distance moved by the compound / distance moved by the solvent front, and is always less than 1.

questions.question: A TLC spot travels 4.5 cm while the solvent front travels 9.0 cm. What is the Rf value?
In paper chromatography, the stationary phase is best described as:
options: The dry cellulose fibres of the paper alone
Water held within the cellulose fibres of the paper
The solvent in the developing tank
The pencil line used to spot the sample
questions.correct_answer: Water held within the cellulose fibres of the paper
questions.explanation: In paper chromatography the true stationary phase is the layer of water adsorbed onto the cellulose fibres, while the mobile phase is the developing solvent.

questions.question: In column chromatography, the sample components that are LEAST strongly adsorbed onto the stationary phase (packing material) will:
options: Remain permanently at the top of the column
Elute (come off the column) first
Elute last, after all other components
Never separate from the mobile phase
questions.correct_answer: Elute (come off the column) first
questions.explanation: Weakly retained components move fastest with the mobile phase and are collected first at the bottom of the column; strongly adsorbed components elute later.

questions.question: Liquid-liquid extraction (using a separating funnel) relies on the principle that a solute distributes between two immiscible solvents according to its:
options: Melting point in each solvent
Partition (distribution) coefficient between the two solvents
Electrical charge in each solvent
Density relative to water only
questions.correct_answer: Partition (distribution) coefficient between the two solvents
questions.explanation: A solute distributes between two immiscible liquids in a ratio described by its partition coefficient, which extraction exploits to transfer it preferentially into one phase.

questions.question: When using a separating funnel for extraction, why must the tap be opened periodically (with the funnel inverted) during shaking?
options: To mix the layers more vigorously
To release built-up vapour pressure from volatile solvents and prevent the stopper from being forced out
To add more solvent to the funnel
To check the colour of the lower layer
questions.correct_answer: To release built-up vapour pressure from volatile solvents and prevent the stopper from being forced out
questions.explanation: Shaking immiscible, often volatile solvents builds internal pressure; venting through the tap at intervals prevents pressure buildup that could pop the stopper or burst the funnel.

questions.question: Simple distillation is an appropriate technique for separating:
options: Two miscible liquids with very close boiling points
A dissolved non-volatile solute (e.g. salt) from a volatile solvent (e.g. water)
Two immiscible liquids of similar density
A mixture of solids only
questions.correct_answer: A dissolved non-volatile solute (e.g. salt) from a volatile solvent (e.g. water)
questions.explanation: Simple distillation vaporizes and condenses a volatile liquid away from a non-volatile dissolved solid or from a liquid with a very different, well-separated boiling point.

questions.question: Fractional distillation differs from simple distillation mainly by the addition of a:
options: Fractionating column providing repeated vaporization-condensation cycles to separate liquids with close boiling points
Larger heating mantle for higher temperatures
Second condenser in series
Vacuum pump to lower the pressure
questions.correct_answer: Fractionating column providing repeated vaporization-condensation cycles to separate liquids with close boiling points
questions.explanation: The fractionating column provides a large surface area for repeated condensation and re-vaporization, improving separation of liquids whose boiling points are close together.

questions.question: Steam distillation is particularly useful for isolating a volatile, heat-sensitive compound (e.g. an essential oil) that is immiscible with water because:
options: It allows the compound to distil at a temperature below its normal boiling point, avoiding decomposition
It requires no heating at all
It increases the boiling point of the compound above 100 degC
It only works with water-soluble compounds
questions.correct_answer: It allows the compound to distil at a temperature below its normal boiling point, avoiding decomposition
questions.explanation: With immiscible liquids, the mixture boils when the sum of the two vapour pressures equals atmospheric pressure, so the compound co-distils with steam at a temperature below its own boiling point.

questions.question: Crystallization is used to purify a solid compound mainly by exploiting:
options: Its differential solubility in a solvent at high versus low temperature
Its boiling point in the pure state
Its electrical conductivity in solution
Its colour under ultraviolet light
questions.correct_answer: Its differential solubility in a solvent at high versus low temperature
questions.explanation: The compound is dissolved in a minimum volume of hot solvent, then slowly cooled so it becomes less soluble and crystallizes out, leaving soluble impurities in solution.

questions.question: Adding a small 'seed' crystal to a cooled, supersaturated solution helps to:
options: Dissolve any remaining solid completely
Initiate and promote ordered crystal growth rather than a sudden, uncontrolled precipitate
Raise the boiling point of the solution
Neutralize the solution's pH
questions.correct_answer: Initiate and promote ordered crystal growth rather than a sudden, uncontrolled precipitate
questions.explanation: A seed crystal provides a nucleation site so the solute deposits in an ordered lattice, producing larger, purer crystals rather than rapid, impure precipitation.

questions.question: A good recrystallization solvent for a given compound should ideally:
options: Dissolve the compound well when cold and remain insoluble when hot
Dissolve the compound well when hot but only sparingly when cold, so crystals form on cooling
Be completely unable to dissolve the compound at any temperature
React chemically with the compound to form a new substance
questions.correct_answer: Dissolve the compound well when hot but only sparingly when cold, so crystals form on cooling
questions.explanation: An ideal recrystallization solvent gives high solubility of the compound at its boiling point and low solubility when cold, maximizing recovery of pure crystals.

questions.question: Sublimation is used as a purification method for compounds that:
options: Boil at very low temperatures only
Pass directly from the solid to the gaseous state (and back) without melting, leaving non-sublimable impurities behind
Are highly soluble in water at room temperature
Decompose immediately on any heating
questions.correct_answer: Pass directly from the solid to the gaseous state (and back) without melting, leaving non-sublimable impurities behind
questions.explanation: Sublimable solids (e.g. iodine, naphthalene) vaporize directly and re-condense as pure solid on a cold surface, separating them from impurities that do not sublime.

questions.question: 'Drying to constant weight' in the laboratory means a sample is repeatedly dried and reweighed until:
options: It reaches exactly 100 g
Successive weighings show no further significant change in mass, confirming all moisture/volatiles have been removed
The sample changes colour
One hour of drying has elapsed, regardless of the reading
questions.correct_answer: Successive weighings show no further significant change in mass, confirming all moisture/volatiles have been removed
questions.explanation: Constant weight is reached when repeated drying-cooling-weighing cycles produce essentially identical mass readings, showing that drying is complete.

questions.question: A wet sample weighs 12.50 g before drying and 10.00 g after drying to constant weight. What is the percentage moisture content?
questions.explanation: % moisture = (mass lost / initial mass) x 100 = (2.50/12.50) x 100 = 20.0%.

questions.question: The main difference between evaporation and distillation as separation techniques is that:
options: Evaporation recovers only the solvent vapour, while distillation is used only for solids
Evaporation is used to obtain the dissolved solid by driving off the solvent (which is usually lost), while distillation condenses and collects the vaporized liquid itself
There is no real difference between the two techniques
Evaporation always requires a vacuum, unlike distillation
questions.correct_answer: Evaporation is used to obtain the dissolved solid by driving off the solvent (which is usually lost), while distillation condenses and collects the vaporized liquid itself
questions.explanation: Evaporation simply drives off solvent to concentrate or isolate a solute, whereas distillation specifically condenses and collects the vapour as a purified liquid product.

questions.question: The general steps of a gravimetric analysis, in correct order, are:
options: Precipitate the analyte, filter, wash, dry/ignite to constant weight, then weigh the precipitate
Weigh the sample, dissolve it, and report the mass directly as the analyte
Titrate the sample, then evaporate the titrant
Filter first, then add the precipitating reagent afterward
questions.correct_answer: Precipitate the analyte, filter, wash, dry/ignite to constant weight, then weigh the precipitate
questions.explanation: Gravimetric analysis quantifies an analyte by converting it to an insoluble precipitate, then filtering, washing, drying/igniting, and weighing it to determine mass and hence composition.

questions.question: In gravimetric analysis, the precipitate is washed with a suitable wash liquid (not pure water alone, in many cases) mainly to:
options: Increase the mass of the precipitate
Remove soluble impurities/adsorbed ions from the precipitate surface without causing it to dissolve or peptize
Dissolve the precipitate completely for easier transfer
Change the precipitate's chemical identity
questions.correct_answer: Remove soluble impurities/adsorbed ions from the precipitate surface without causing it to dissolve or peptize
questions.explanation: An appropriate wash solution removes surface-adsorbed impurities while minimizing solubility loss of the precipitate and preventing peptization (breakup into colloidal particles).

questions.question: If a reaction theoretically should yield 5.00 g of product but only 4.25 g is actually obtained, the percentage yield is:
questions.explanation: % yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) x 100 = (4.25/5.00) x 100 = 85.0%.

questions.question: A sample of crude compound weighing 8.0 g is found to contain 6.4 g of the pure active substance. What is the percentage purity of the sample?
questions.explanation: % purity = (mass of pure substance / total sample mass) x 100 = (6.4/8.0) x 100 = 80.0%.

questions.question: In colorimetry/spectrophotometry, the basic principle used to determine the concentration of a coloured solution is that:
options: Concentration is directly proportional to the solution's boiling point
The amount of light absorbed by the solution is related to the concentration of the absorbing substance, as described by the Beer-Lambert law
Concentration is measured by weighing the coloured solution
Colour intensity has no relationship to concentration
questions.correct_answer: The amount of light absorbed by the solution is related to the concentration of the absorbing substance, as described by the Beer-Lambert law
questions.explanation: Colorimetry and spectrophotometry measure light absorbance, which the Beer-Lambert law relates directly to the concentration of the coloured/absorbing species in solution.

questions.question: The Beer-Lambert law is commonly expressed as A = ecl. In this equation, 'c' represents:
options: The path length of light through the sample
The molar absorptivity (extinction coefficient) of the substance
The concentration of the absorbing solution
The wavelength of light used
questions.correct_answer: The concentration of the absorbing solution
questions.explanation: In A = ecl, A is absorbance, e (epsilon) is the molar absorptivity, c is concentration, and l is the path length of the light through the sample.

questions.question: Before measuring the absorbance of a series of coloured sample solutions, a spectrophotometer is first zeroed using a 'blank'. The blank typically contains:
options: The most concentrated standard solution available
All reagents used in colour development except the analyte itself, to correct for background absorbance
Pure mercury for calibration
A solution of unknown, random composition
questions.correct_answer: All reagents used in colour development except the analyte itself, to correct for background absorbance
questions.explanation: The blank contains the same solvent/reagents as the samples but without the analyte, allowing the instrument to be zeroed against background absorbance from the matrix.

questions.question: Gel electrophoresis separates charged molecules (e.g. DNA fragments or proteins) mainly on the basis of their:
options: Colour under visible light
Size (and charge), as they migrate through a gel matrix under an applied electric field
Melting point
Solubility in organic solvents
questions.correct_answer: Size (and charge), as they migrate through a gel matrix under an applied electric field
questions.explanation: In an electric field, charged molecules migrate through the porous gel matrix at rates influenced chiefly by their size (and charge/shape), separating them into bands.

questions.question: In agarose gel electrophoresis of DNA, smaller DNA fragments migrate:
options: Faster and further through the gel than larger fragments
Slower and less far through the gel than larger fragments
At exactly the same rate as larger fragments
Away from the direction of the electric field
questions.correct_answer: Faster and further through the gel than larger fragments
questions.explanation: Smaller DNA fragments move more easily through the pores of the agarose gel matrix and therefore travel farther than larger fragments in the same run time.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a standard method of preserving a laboratory sample prior to analysis?
options: Refrigeration or freezing to slow decomposition
Addition of an appropriate chemical preservative
Drying or desiccation to remove moisture
Leaving the sample uncovered at room temperature indefinitely
questions.correct_answer: Leaving the sample uncovered at room temperature indefinitely
questions.explanation: Uncovered storage at room temperature promotes contamination, evaporation, and microbial or chemical degradation; recognized preservation methods include cooling, freezing, drying, or adding preservatives.

questions.question: A Soxhlet extractor is a continuous solid-liquid extraction apparatus mainly used to:
options: Extract a soluble compound repeatedly from a solid sample using a small, continuously recycled volume of solvent
Distil two miscible liquids of similar boiling point
Filter a precipitate under vacuum
Measure the pH of a solid sample
questions.correct_answer: Extract a soluble compound repeatedly from a solid sample using a small, continuously recycled volume of solvent
questions.explanation: A Soxhlet apparatus repeatedly floods a solid sample with fresh, condensed solvent, efficiently extracting soluble compounds using a relatively small total solvent volume.

questions.question: A rotary evaporator ('rotavap') is used in the laboratory chiefly to:
options: Efficiently remove solvent from a solution under reduced pressure at a relatively low temperature
Titrate a solution to its end point
Measure the melting point of a solid
Separate ions by electrophoresis
questions.correct_answer: Efficiently remove solvent from a solution under reduced pressure at a relatively low temperature
questions.explanation: The rotary evaporator combines reduced pressure, gentle heating, and rotation to remove solvent quickly while minimizing thermal decomposition of the product.

questions.question: Determining the melting point of a purified solid and comparing it with the literature value is a common technique used mainly to assess:
options: The colour of the compound
The purity and identity of the compound, since impurities typically lower and broaden the melting point range
The exact molecular formula of the compound
The boiling point of the compound
questions.correct_answer: The purity and identity of the compound, since impurities typically lower and broaden the melting point range
questions.explanation: A sharp melting point close to the literature value indicates a pure compound; a lowered, broadened range indicates the presence of impurities.
